Fetch
fĕch
v. (to go and bring; in Scripture the errand of hospitality, the prophet's test of a widow, and the wise woman's word for restoring the banished)
From Anglo-Saxon feccan, to bring — probably a variant of fetian, to go and get. English kept the two-part sense the Hebrew also has: fetch is not merely to bring but to go and bring.

Biblical Definition

Fetch is a servant's verb, and Scripture puts it in some surprising mouths. Abraham uses it of himself at Mamre, running the errand for his own guests: “I will fetch a morsel of bread, and comfort ye your hearts” (Gen 18:5) — and the morsel turns into a calf, cakes, butter and milk, the pattern of hospitality that promises little and gives much. Elijah uses it as a test of a widow at the end of her resources: “Fetch me, I pray thee, a little water in a vessel, that I may drink” (1Ki 17:10), the first of three requests that would each cost her more than the last. The Law uses it to protect the poor from a creditor's intrusion: “When thou dost lend thy brother any thing, thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge” (Deu 24:10) — a man's home is not open to his lender. And the wise woman of Tekoa uses it for the restoration of an exile, in the sentence that persuades David about Absalom: “the king doth not fetch home again his banished” (2Sa 14:13).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines fetch as to go and bring; to bring, to go for and produce — and also, to bring back, to recall, and to derive or draw from a source.

expand to see more

FETCH, v.t. To go and bring; to go and take from a place, and bring to another.

Fetch me, I pray thee, a little water in a vessel. 1 Kings xvii.

2. To derive; to draw, as from a source.

3. To bring back; to recall; to bring to any state; as, to fetch a man to life.

4. To reach; to arrive at; to come to; as, the ship fetched the port.

Key Scripture

Gen 18:5 — "And I will fetch a morsel of bread, and comfort ye your hearts; after that ye shall pass on: for therefore are ye come to your servant. And they said, So do, as thou hast said."

1Ki 17:10 — "So he arose and went to Zarephath. And when he came to the gate of the city, behold, the widow woman was there gathering of sticks: and he called to her, and said, Fetch me, I pray thee, a little water in a vessel, that I may drink."

Deu 24:10 — "When thou dost lend thy brother any thing, thou shalt not go into his house to fetch his pledge."

2Sa 14:13 — "And the woman said, Wherefore then hast thou thought such a thing against the people of God? for the king doth speak this thing as one which is faulty, in that the king doth not fetch home again his banished."

Modern Corruption

The Zarephath narrative is turned into a seed-faith parable — give the prophet your last meal and God will multiply your money — which mistakes a famine miracle for a financial method.

expand to see more

1Ki 17 is one of the most heavily abused passages in the prosperity repertoire: the widow gives her last handful to the man of God, and the barrel of meal does not waste. Preached as a principle, it becomes a fundraising instrument — sow into this ministry from your poverty and expect return. But the text is a famine narrative in which a Gentile widow is sustained day by day, not enriched; the meal and the oil last exactly as long as the drought and no longer, and her son dies in the next paragraph. Whatever else the chapter teaches, it does not teach that giving is an investment vehicle.

What it does teach is the sovereign extension of mercy beyond Israel, which is precisely how the Lord Jesus used it in the synagogue at Nazareth — many widows were in Israel, and to none of them was Elijah sent, but to Sarepta (Luk 4:25-26) — and the congregation tried to throw Him off a cliff for saying so. Deu 24:10 shows the same God protecting the poor in ordinary law: a creditor may take a pledge but may not walk into a man's house to fetch it, and if the pledge is his cloak it goes back before sundown. That is what care for the poor looks like in Scripture: enforceable limits on the powerful, not a promise of returns to the desperate.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Anglo-Saxon feccan, to go and bring; rendering Hebrew laqach (H3947), to take, and bo (H935) in the causative, to bring.

expand to see more

Anglo-Saxon feccan — to go and bring; the errand and the carrying are both in the word.

Hebrew laqach (H3947) — to take, fetch, receive; “I will fetch a morsel of bread” (Gen 18:5).

Hebrew bo (H935), hiphil hebi — to cause to come, to bring; “fetch me… a little water” (1Ki 17:10).

Hebrew shub (H7725), hiphil — to bring back; “fetch home again his banished” (2Sa 14:13), the verb of restoration and of repentance alike.

Hebrew abot (H5667) — a pledge given for a loan; the thing the creditor may not enter a house to fetch (Deu 24:10).

Usage

"“I will fetch a morsel of bread” — and set before them a calf, cakes, butter and milk."

"“Fetch me… a little water” — the first of three requests, each costlier than the last."

"“Doth not fetch home again his banished” — a wise woman's word for restoration."
